==Problem==
What is the tens digit of <imath>7^{2011}</imath>?

<imath> \textbf{(A) }0\qquad\textbf{(B) }1\qquad\textbf{(C) }3\qquad\textbf{(D) }4\qquad\textbf{(E) }7 </imath>

==Solution 1==
Since we want the tens digit, we can find the last two digits of <imath>7^{2011}</imath>.  We can do this by using modular arithmetic.
<cmath>7^1\equiv 07 \pmod{100}.</cmath>
<cmath>7^2\equiv 49 \pmod{100}.</cmath>
<cmath>7^3\equiv 43 \pmod{100}.</cmath>
<cmath>7^4\equiv 01 \pmod{100}.</cmath>
We can write <imath>7^{2011}</imath> as <imath>(7^4)^{502}\times 7^3</imath>.  Using this, we can say:
<cmath>7^{2011}\equiv (7^4)^{502}\times 7^3\equiv 7^3\equiv 343\equiv 43\pmod{100}.</cmath>
From the above, we can conclude that the last two digits of <imath>7^{2011}</imath> are 43.  Since they have asked us to find the tens digit, our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}\ 4}</imath>.

-Ilovefruits

==Solution 2==
The last two digits of <imath>7^{2011}</imath> can be found by taking <imath>\pmod{100}</imath> of <imath>7^{2011}</imath>. By [[Euler's Totient Theorem]], we have that <imath>7^{\phi(100)}\equiv 7^{40}\equiv 1 \pmod{100}</imath>, so we can conclude that <imath>7^{2011} \equiv 7^{40^{50}} \cdot 7^{11}\equiv 7^{11} \pmod{100}</imath>. We can find that the modular inverse of <imath>7 \pmod{100}</imath> is <imath>43</imath>, and since <imath>7^{12}\equiv 01 \pmod{100}</imath>, we can conclude that <imath>7^{11}\equiv 7^{12} \cdot 7^{-1}\equiv 1 \cdot 43\equiv 43 \pmod{100}</imath>. The problem asked for the tens digit, so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}\ 4}</imath>.
~Baihly2024
